summary: Sets out conventions for digitally signing Internet-Drafts. It uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax to make a detached signature stored in a separate companion file, so existing tools that handle drafts keep working unchanged.

eli5.summary: A signature on a paper proves who wrote it. This note says how to make a digital signature for a draft document and keep it in a second file, so the draft itself stays untouched.

questions: what is a detached cms signature
how to verify an internet-draft signature
subtitle: How the IETF Secretariat signs each Internet-Draft with a detached CMS signature in a companion file.

tldr.problem: Anyone holding a copy of an Internet-Draft has no simple way to confirm it is the document the IETF Secretariat posted, and the fix must not break the tools that already handle drafts.
tldr.mechanism: The Secretariat creates a detached Cryptographic Message Syntax signature over the canonicalized draft and posts it as a companion file with the same name plus .p7s.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can check that a draft is unaltered since it was posted. The signing time is wall-clock time, not a trusted timestamp. This memo was later updated by RFC 8358.

facts.label: Signature file suffix
facts.value: .p7s added to the draft file name

today: RFC 5485 is an Informational RFC published in March 2009 and has been updated by RFC 8358. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Signing Internet-Drafts
sections.content:
Shortly after the IETF Secretariat posts an Internet-Draft in the repository, it generates a digital signature and posts it as a companion file in the same repository. The signature lets anyone confirm that the contents have not been altered since the draft was posted.

The signature is a detached CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) signature stored separately, so no existing utilities are affected. The signing time included is wall-clock time and is not meant to be a trusted timestamp.
sections.eli5: The draft gets a matching sealed note kept in a separate envelope. If the draft changes, the note will no longer match.

sections.title: The Signature File and Canonicalization
sections.content:
The signature file has exactly the same name as the draft with .p7s added, for example draft-ietf-example-widgets-03.txt and draft-ietf-example-widgets-03.txt.p7s. File names are the only link between the two, so the pair can be stored anywhere.

Plain text needs canonicalization first, because operating systems mark line ends differently. The rules follow FTP text conventions: 8-bit NVT-ASCII, CRLF at every line end, no trailing spaces on a line and no trailing blank lines at the end of the file. Nonprintable and non-ASCII characters (outside 0x20 to 0x7E) MUST NOT be changed beyond the line-end rules, and operating system end-of-file markers are not signed.

XML files use a single LF for line ends. Other formats need no canonicalization and are signed as plain octets.
sections.eli5: Computers write the end of a line differently, so everyone first tidies the draft the same way. Then the signature matches no matter whose computer checks it.

sections.title: The CMS Profile
sections.content:
The outer wrapper is a ContentInfo that MUST hold a SignedData value. Because the signature is detached, eContent MUST be absent. Both SignedData and SignerInfo use version 3, and exactly one signer, the IETF Secretariat, is expected, although more than one SignerInfo MAY appear to ease key or algorithm changes. The certificate SHOULD be included, and CRLs SHOULD NOT be.

The signed attributes are required and DER-encoded. The Secretariat MUST include content-type, message-digest and signing-time, and MAY add binary-signing-time. Since signing may be done in batches, the signing time can be hours or days after posting. Unsigned attributes are usually omitted but MAY hold a trusted timestamp.

Each file format has its own content type, listed below. The same value appears in eContentType and in the content-type attribute.
sections.eli5: The signed envelope has a fixed list of what goes inside: who signed, when, a fingerprint of the draft, and what kind of file it was.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
The Secretariat MUST protect its private key, and a hardware security module (HSM) is strongly RECOMMENDED because a compromised key permits masquerade. The two servers (primary and backup) need two HSMs, which do not have to share a key if each has its own certificate. The HSM ought to be owned by the IETF Trust.

Algorithms weaken with time, so it SHOULD be possible to migrate them. Weak random number generation can make key pairs guessable. Signing in batches allows the HSM to stay offline except when signing, and allows manual steps such as entering a passphrase.
sections.eli5: The signing stamp is kept in a locked safe. If someone stole it, they could fake notes, so it gets guarded very carefully.

sections.title: Design Rationale and Verification
sections.content:
A detached signature is used for every format, even PDF and XML, which have their own signing methods. One method is simpler for the Secretariat to implement, and an author's own signature is not harmed by it. Linking by file name, rather than a signed attribute, lets a draft and its signature be stored anywhere, which matters for validating expired drafts obtained from non-IETF repositories.

The appendix shows a check with OpenSSL 0.9.9 using openssl cms -verify, a trust anchor certificate file, the canonicalized draft and the DER-encoded .p7s file.
sections.eli5: Keeping the signature in its own file means you can copy the draft and its signature to any place and still check them.
